title.en: The Fall of the Watchers (1 Enoch)
title.zh: 守望者之墮落（以諾一書）

region.zh: 黑門山（阿爾孟，安黎巴嫩山）

texts.period: 1 Enoch (Book of the Watchers), c. 3rd c. BCE; trans. Laurence, 1883

source.work: The Book of Enoch the Prophet, trans. Richard Laurence, chs. 7-10

summary.en: The most influential of the pseudepigrapha, quoted in the Epistle of Jude and treasured in the Ethiopian canon: two hundred Watchers, led by Samyaza, swear an oath on Mount Hermon, take the daughters of men, and teach forbidden crafts; their giant offspring fill the earth with blood until the archangels plead for judgment.
summary.zh: 偽經中最具影響力之作，為猶大書所引、埃提阿伯正典所藏：二百守望者由薩麥拉率領，於黑門山立誓，娶人間女子，傳授禁術；其巨人後裔使大地遍染血污，直至天使長呼求審判。

sensitivity.note: Jewish pseudepigraphon preserved in Ge'ez; scriptural for the Ethiopian Orthodox canon, quoted in the New Testament. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: It happened after the sons of men had multiplied in those days, that daughters were born to them, elegant and beautiful. And when the angels, the sons of heaven, beheld them, they became enamoured of them, saying to each other, Come, let us select for ourselves wives from the progeny of men, and let us beget children. [...] Then they swore all together, and all bound themselves by mutual execrations. Their whole number was two hundred, who descended upon Ardis, which is the top of mount Armon. [...] Then they took wives, each choosing for himself; whom they began to approach, and with whom they cohabited; teaching them sorcery, incantations, and the dividing of roots and trees. And the women conceiving brought forth giants, Whose stature was each three hundred cubits.

Moreover Azazyel taught men to make swords, knives, shields, breastplates, the fabrication of mirrors, and the workmanship of bracelets and ornaments, the use of paint, the beautifying of the eyebrows, the use of stones of every valuable and select kind, and of all sorts of dyes, so that the world became altered. Impiety increased; fornication multiplied; and they transgressed and corrupted all their ways. [...] And men, being destroyed, cried out; and their voice reached to heaven.

Then Michael and Gabriel, Raphael, Suryal, and Uriel, looked down from heaven, and saw the quantity of blood which was shed on earth, and all the iniquity which was done upon it, and said one to another, It is the voice of their cries; The earth deprived of her children has cried even to the gate of heaven. [...] The women likewise have brought forth giants. Thus has the whole earth been filled with blood and with iniquity. And now behold the souls of those who are dead, cry out. And complain even to the gate of heaven.

title.en: Enoch's Vision of the Son of Man

region.zh: 以諾比喻篇（異象之境，象徵位置）

texts.period: 1 Enoch (Parables), c. 1st c. BCE; trans. Laurence, 1883

source.work: The Book of Enoch the Prophet, trans. Richard Laurence, ch. 46

summary.en: In the Parables of Enoch the seer beholds the Ancient of days, whose head is like white wool, and with him the Son of man to whom righteousness belongs, chosen by the Lord of spirits to reveal the hidden treasures and to raise up kings from their couches — the messianic vision that shaped Second Temple expectation and New Testament language.
summary.zh: 以諾比喻篇中，先知見「日子古老者」髮如白羊毛，其旁有人子——義所歸焉、為萬靈之主所揀選者，將啟示隱藏之寶藏，並使君王自榻興起——此彌賽亞異象塑造了第二聖殿時代的盼望與新約語言。

sensitivity.note: Jewish pseudepigraphon; the Parables' messianic vision influenced apocalyptic belief across Judaism and Christianity. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There I beheld the Ancient of days, whose head was like white wool, and with him another, whose countenance resembled that of man. His countenance was full of grace, like that of one of the holy angels. Then I inquired of one of the angels, who went with me, and who showed me every secret thing, concerning this Son of man; who he was; whence he was; and why he accompanied the Ancient of days. He answered and said to me, This is the Son of man, to whom righteousness belongs; with whom righteousness has dwelt; and who will reveal all the treasures of that which is concealed: for the Lord of spirits has chosen him; and his portion has surpassed all before the Lord of spirits in everlasting uprightness. This Son of man, whom thou beholdest, shall raise up kings and the mighty from their couches, and the powerful from their thrones; shall loosen the bridles of the powerful, and break in pieces the teeth of sinners.

title.en: Tobit and the Fish of Healing

region.zh: 尼尼微至厄克巴坦（亞述至瑪代）

texts.period: Book of Tobit, c. 2nd c. BCE (deuterocanonical); KJV Apocrypha, 1611

source.work: Bible (King James Version), Apocrypha: Tobit, chs. 6-12

summary.en: Blinded for burying the dead, Tobit sends his son to Media with the angel Raphael in disguise; a fish of the Tigris, caught at the angel's word, supplies the heart and liver whose smoke binds the demon Asmodeus and the gall that heals Tobit's eyes — the deuterocanonical book beloved for its angelology and its teaching on almsgiving.
summary.zh: 多比因埋葬死者而目盲，遣子多比亞往瑪代；拉斐爾天使假伴同行，於底格里斯河捕魚——魚心肝之煙驅逐惡魔阿斯摩太，魚膽醫愈多比之目。此次經典以天使論與施捨教訓聞名。

sensitivity.note: Deuterocanonical/Apocryphal book — canonical for Catholic and Orthodox traditions, apocryphal in Protestantism. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: And when the young man went down to wash himself, a fish leaped out of the river, and would have devoured him. Then the angel said unto him, Take the fish. And the young man laid hold of the fish, and drew it to land. [...] And he said unto him, Touching the heart and the liver, if a devil or an evil spirit trouble any, we must make a smoke thereof before the man or the woman, and the party shall be no more vexed. As for the gall, it is good to anoint a man that hath whiteness in his eyes, and he shall be healed.

And when they had supped, they brought Tobias in unto her. And as he went, he remembered the words of Raphael, and took the ashes of the perfumes, and put the heart and the liver of the fish thereupon, and made a smoke therewith. The which smell when the evil spirit had smelled, he fled into the utmost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.

I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and which go in and out before the glory of the Holy One. [...] For not of any favour of mine, but by the will of our God I came; wherefore praise him for ever.

title.en: Mattathias and the Rededication of the Altar
title.zh: 瑪他提亞與祭壇之重新奉獻

region.zh: 猶太地摩丁與耶路撒冷

texts.period: 1 Maccabees, c. 2nd-1st c. BCE (deuterocanonical); KJV Apocrypha, 1611

source.work: Bible (King James Version), Apocrypha: 1 Maccabees, chs. 2-4

summary.en: The book that records the Maccabean revolt: Antiochus Epiphanes profanes the temple, Mattathias refuses the king's commandment — 'We will not hearken to the king's words, to go from our religion' — and after Judas Maccabeus overthrows the king's host, the sanctuary is cleansed and the altar dedicated anew for eight days, the origin of the feast of Hanukkah.
summary.zh: 記載瑪加伯起義之經卷：安提阿古·伊皮法尼褻瀆聖殿；瑪他提亞拒王命——「不聽王言，不棄祖教」；猶大·瑪加伯破敵之後，潔淨聖所，重新奉獻祭壇八日——修殿節（光明節）之緣起。

sensitivity.note: Deuterocanonical/Apocryphal book — canonical for Catholic and Orthodox traditions, historically foundational for the Jewish feast of Hanukkah. Presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Then Mattathias answered and spake with a loud voice, Though all the nations that are under the king's dominion obey him, and fall away every one from the religion of their fathers, and give consent to his commandments: Yet will I and my sons and my brethren walk in the covenant of our fathers. God forbid that we should forsake the law and the ordinances. We will not hearken to the king's words, to go from our religion, either on the right hand, or the left.

Then said Judas to the men that were with him, Fear ye not their multitude, neither be ye afraid of their assault. Remember how our fathers were delivered in the Red sea, when Pharaoh pursued them with an army. [...] For the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host; but strength cometh from heaven.

Now on the five and twentieth day of the ninth month, which is called the month Casleu, in the hundred forty and eighth year, they rose up betimes in the morning, And offered sacrifice according to the law upon the new altar of burnt offerings, which they had made. Look, at what time and what day the heathen had profaned it, even in that was it dedicated with songs, and citherns, and harps, and cymbals. [...] And so they kept the dedication of the altar eight days, and offered burnt offerings with gladness, and sacrificed the sacrifice of deliverance and praise.

title.en: Dante's Inferno: The Gate and the Lovers
title.zh: 但丁《神曲·地獄篇》：冥門與情人

region.zh: 義大利佛羅倫斯／幽暗森林（異象之境）

texts.period: Divine Comedy, c. 1308-1320; trans. Henry Francis Cary, 1805-14

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Hell (Inferno), Cantos 1, 3, 5

summary.en: Dante's pilgrimage through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise — the poem that shaped the Western imagination of the afterlife: lost in a dark wood at mid-life, he passes the gate whose doomful lines end 'All hope abandon ye who enter here,' and hears the lovers Francesca and Paolo tell how the book of Lancelot betrayed them to their love.
summary.zh: 但丁遊歷地獄、煉獄與天堂——塑造西方死後想像之詩：半生迷途於幽暗森林，過地獄之門（門上銘文云：「入此門者，當捨棄一切希望」），聞弗蘭切斯卡與保羅情人敘述蘭斯洛特之書如何使其墮入情網。

sensitivity.note: Influential Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); presented as a comparative text alongside underworld-journey narratives — a scholarly framing.

passages.text: In the midway of this our mortal life, I found me in a gloomy wood, astray Gone from the path direct: and e'en to tell It were no easy task, how savage wild That forest, how robust and rough its growth, Which to remember only, my dismay Renews, in bitterness not far from death.

"Through me you pass into the city of woe: Through me you pass into eternal pain: Through me among the people lost for aye. Justice the founder of my fabric mov'd: To rear me was the task of power divine, Supremest wisdom, and primeval love. Before me things create were none, save things Eternal, and eternal I endure. "All hope abandon ye who enter here."

"Love, that in gentle heart is quickly learnt, Entangled him by that fair form, from me Ta'en in such cruel sort, as grieves me still: Love, that denial takes from none belov'd, Caught me with pleasing him so passing well, That, as thou see'st, he yet deserts me not. Love brought us to one death: Caina waits The soul, who spilt our life." [...] "No greater grief than to remember days Of joy, when mis'ry is at hand! [...] The book and writer both Were love's purveyors. In its leaves that day We read no more."

title.en: Milton's Paradise Lost: The Fall of the Rebel Angels
title.zh: 彌爾頓《失樂園》：叛天使之墮落

source.work: Paradise Lost, John Milton, Book I

summary.en: Milton's epic of the fall — 'to justify the ways of God to men' — opens with Satan and his legions hurled from heaven through nine days' space into a dungeon of darkness visible; waking on the burning lake, the Arch-fiend rallies his fallen host and builds Pandemonium, resolving on 'war, then, war, open or understood.'
summary.zh: 彌爾頓之史詩——「辯明上帝待人之道」——敘撒旦與其黨羽九日九夜自天墮落，墜入「可見之黑暗」深淵；於火湖醒來，召集墮落天使，建萬魔殿，立誓「戰爭——明戰或暗戰，勢不可免」。

sensitivity.note: Influential Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); the epic paraphrases the apocryphal angelologies of Enoch and shaped Protestant imagination. Presented as a comparative text.

passages.text: Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste Brought death into the World, and all our woe, With loss of Eden, till one greater Man Restore us, and regain the blissful seat, Sing, Heavenly Muse [...] That, to the height of this great argument, I may assert Eternal Providence, And justify the ways of God to men.

Th' infernal Serpent; he it was whose guile, Stirred up with envy and revenge, deceived The mother of mankind [...] Him the Almighty Power Hurled headlong flaming from th' ethereal sky, With hideous ruin and combustion, down To bottomless perdition, there to dwell In adamantine chains and penal fire, Who durst defy th' Omnipotent to arms.

A dungeon horrible, on all sides round, As one great furnace flamed; yet from those flames No light; but rather darkness visible Served only to discover sights of woe [...] Here at least We shall be free; th' Almighty hath not built Here for his envy, will not drive us hence: Here we may reign secure; and, in my choice, To reign is worth ambition, though in Hell: Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.

title.en: The Song of the Reed (Masnavi of Rumi)
title.zh: 蘆笛之歌（魯米《瑪斯納維》）

region.zh: 安納托利亞科尼亞（魯米旋轉祈禱之家）

texts.period: Masnavi, Book 1, c. 1258-1273; trans. E. H. Whinfield (abridged), 1887

source.work: Masnavi I Ma'navi, trans. E. H. Whinfield, Book I Prologue

summary.en: The Masnavi — the Sufi 'Qur'an in the Persian tongue,' read for eight centuries across the Muslim world — opens with the reed-flute cut from its osier bed, wailing for its home: the soul torn from the Source, whose fire of love is the physician of pride, the confidant of all unhappy lovers.
summary.zh: 《瑪斯納維》——蘇菲「波斯語之古蘭經」，八百年來穆斯林世界誦讀不絕——以蘆笛自葦床剪斷、哀鳴思鄉為喻：靈魂離其本源，愛之火乃傲慢之醫、苦戀者之知己。

sensitivity.note: Influential Sufi literature of Islam (not scripture); presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains, Lamenting its banishment from its home: "Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears. I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs, And to express the pangs of my yearning for my home. He who abides far away from his home Is ever longing for the day he shall return. [...] My secrets are not alien from my plaintive notes, Yet they are not manifest to the sensual eye and ear. Body is not veiled from soul, neither soul from body, Yet no man hath ever seen a soul." This plaint of the flute is fire, not mere air. Let him who lacks this fire be accounted dead! 'Tis the fire of love that inspires the flute, 'Tis the ferment of love that possesses the wine.

The pitcher of the desire of the covetous never fills, The oyster-shell fills not with pearls till it is content; Only he whose garment is rent by the violence of love Is wholly pure from covetousness and sin. Hail to thee, then, O LOVE, sweet madness! Thou who healest all our infirmities! Who art the physician of our pride and self-conceit! Who art our Plato and our Galen! Love exalts our earthly bodies to heaven, And makes the very hills to dance with joy!

title.en: The Cosmic Egg and the Sleep of Vishnu (Vishnu Purana)
title.zh: 宇宙之卵與毗濕奴之眠（毗濕奴往世書）

region.zh: 印度庫魯克謝特拉（敘述之地）

texts.period: Vishnu Purana, c. 1st millennium CE; trans. H. H. Wilson, 1840

source.work: The Vishnu Purana, trans. H. H. Wilson, Book I, chs. 1-2

summary.en: The Purana that Wilson called the most authentic of the eighteen: the world was produced from Vishnu, exists in him, and he is the world; the elements combine to form the vast egg that is the abode of Vishnu in the form of Brahma — and at the close of each kalpa, as Rudra, he swallows up the universe and reposes on the serpent-couch, to create again.
summary.zh: 威爾遜譽為十八往世書中最可信者：世界自毗濕奴而生、存於其中，彼即世界；諸元素結合成大卵，乃毗濕奴現梵天之身而居之——每一劫末，彼現為魯陀羅吞滅宇宙，偃臥巨蛇之榻，而後再造。

sensitivity.note: Influential Puranic cosmology of Hinduism; presented as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The world was produced from Vishnu: it exists in him: he is the cause of its continuance and cessation; he is the world. [...] Who can describe him who is not to be apprehended by the senses: who is the best of all things; the supreme soul, self-existent: who is devoid of all the distinguishing characteristics of complexion, caste, or the like; and is exempt from bulk, vicissitude, death, or decay: who is always, and alone: who exists everywhere, and in whom all things here exist; and who is, thence, named Vasudeva? [...] He is Brahma, Supreme, lord, eternal, unborn, imperishable, undecaying; of one essence; ever pure, as free from defects. He, that Brahma, was all things; comprehending in his own nature the indiscrete and discrete.

Having combined, therefore, with one another, they assumed, through their mutual association, the character of one mass of entire unity; and, from the direction of spirit, with the acquiescence of the indiscrete Principle, Intellect and the rest, to the gross elements inclusive, formed an egg, which gradually expanded like a bubble of water. This vast egg, O sage, compounded of the elements, and resting on the waters, was the excellent natural abode of Vishnu in the form of Brahma [...] In that egg, O Brahman, were the continents and seas and mountains, the planets and divisions of the universe, the gods, the demons, and mankind.

Vishnu, with the quality of goodness, and of immeasurable power, preserves created things through successive ages, until the close of the period termed a Kalpa; when the same mighty deity, Janardana, invested with the quality of darkness, assumes the awful form of Rudra, and swallows up the universe. Having thus devoured all things, and converted the world into one vast ocean, the Supreme reposes upon his mighty serpent-couch amidst the deep: he awakes after a season, and, again, as Brahma, becomes the author of creation.
